title: Cofibrant degreewise groupoid completion preserves the diagonal nerve
statement:
Use simplicial sets [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-set] and weak homotopy equivalences [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper]. Fix a small set $O$. A simplicial category $C$ on $O$ consists of simplicial mapping sets $C(a,b)$, associative simplicial composition, and identity vertices. Give these categories and the functors fixing $O$ the fixed-object model structure obtained from the $O\times O$-sorted algebraic theory of composition and units [lem-coef-sorted-simplicial-algebra-model]; weak equivalences and fibrations are detected on all mapping simplicial sets. Let $C$ be cofibrant in this structure. Define $G(C)$ by groupoid-completing the ordinary category $C_q$ of degree-$q$ arrows for each $q$, adjoining formal inverses to all arrows and imposing composition and inverse relations, with simplicial operators induced by the universal properties. For any simplicial category $V$ on $O$, its bisimplicial nerve has
$$B(V)_{p,q}=\coprod_{x_0,\ldots,x_p\in O}\prod_{i=1}^{p}V(x_{i-1},x_i)_q.$$
The operators in $p$ compose adjacent arrows or omit an end arrow, and insert identity arrows for degeneracies; operators in $q$ are those of the mapping sets. An empty product is a singleton. Write $NV=\operatorname{diag}B(V)$, so $(NV)_n=B(V)_{n,n}$. Then the canonical map $NC\to NG(C)$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. There is no assumption that $\pi_0C$ is a groupoid, that mapping simplicial sets are Kan, or that $O$ or the nerve is nonempty or connected.

source.place: Dwyer–Kan, Simplicial localizations of categories, Proposition 9.2 and its proof, printed p.279; nerve in 1.4(vi), completion in 9.1, fixed-object model structure in 7.1–7.2. Read online 2026-10-17; archive WANTED. No Stacks tag states this enriched homotopy theorem.

proof.text: Let $I_O$ be the identity-only category on $O$. For the composition-and-unit sorted theory, the free algebra $F_{xy}(K)$ on a simplicial set $K$ in sort $(x,y)$ is the degreewise path category of the graph with edges $K$ from $x$ to $y$ and no other edges: a simplicial functor out is exactly a simplicial map $K\to C(x,y)$. Apply the boundary small-object factorization in [lem-coef-sorted-simplicial-algebra-model] to $I_O\to C$, obtaining a relative boundary-cell map $j:I_O\to F$ followed by a mappingwise trivial fibration $p:F\to C$. Here is its degreewise description. In degree $q$, the simplices of $\Delta^m$ outside its boundary are exactly the surjections $[q]\twoheadrightarrow[m]$. A pushout of $F_{xy}(\partial\Delta^m)\to F_{xy}(\Delta^m)$ therefore freely adjoins one edge with endpoints $(x,y)$ for each such surjection; the other simplices are assigned to their prescribed old arrows. The pushout universal property verifies that there are no new relations among these new edges and the old category. A coproduct of cells tags these edges by their cells. At a limit stage every arrow is a finite word from preceding stages, so starting with $I_O$, the degree-$q$ category is free on the union of the tagged edges. Thus every $F_q$ is a free category $P(Q_q)$ on a small directed graph $Q_q$ on $O$, also for loops $x=y$ and $m=0$. Cofibrancy of $C$ means that $I_O\to C$ lifts against $p$, giving $i:C\to F$ with $pi=1_C$. No assertion that face maps preserve generators is needed.

source.place: Proposition 9.2 and Section 7.6: free retract reduction; boundary-cell argument written out using the sorted-model node

proof.text: Fix a small directed graph $Q$ on $O$, write $P=P(Q)$ for its path category, and let $u:P\to G(P)$ be completion. Represent arrows of $G(P)$ by composable signed edge words, modulo insertion/deletion of adjacent inverse pairs: expansion of positive paths gives this presentation directly from completion's defining relations. Reduce a word by scanning left to right, cancelling the last stored letter when it is inverse to the next letter and appending otherwise. Appending $e$ and then $e^{-1}$ restores any reduced stack (if the first append cancels, reducedness prevents the second from cancelling again); hence the final output is invariant under each defining relation, also inside a longer word. Each scan deletes only inverse pairs and fixes reduced words, so every arrow has exactly one reduced signed word.

source.place: Proposition 3.7, total inversion special case; Section 3.2 signed-word presentation; agent-supplied comma-tree calculation

proof.text: For $b\in O$, the comma category $E_b=(b\downarrow u)$ has objects the reduced signed words $w:b\to x$ and arrows $w\to w'$ the positive edge words $a:x\to x'$ satisfying $w'=\operatorname{red}(wa)$. Define a directed graph $T_b$ on these objects with an edge $w\to\operatorname{red}(we)$ for each generating edge $e$ out of $x$. A positive word uniquely determines the successive lifted edges by its successive prefixes; conversely a lifted directed path records that positive word. These mutually inverse descriptions preserve concatenation and empty words, so $E_b=P(T_b)$. All sets are small, being sets of finite words in small sets.

source.place: Proposition 3.7, total inversion special case; Section 3.2 signed-word presentation; agent-supplied comma-tree calculation

proof.text: The underlying undirected graph of $T_b$ is a rooted tree, with root the empty word at $b$. Every edge changes length by exactly one, and each nonempty reduced word has precisely one edge to a shorter word: delete its final signed letter (a positive last letter gives an incoming lifted edge, a negative last letter an outgoing one). Thus there are no loops or parallel undirected edges, and a simple cycle would have a maximal-length vertex with two distinct shorter neighbors, impossible. Repeated deletion connects each vertex to the root, proving the tree assertion even when $Q$ has loops or parallel edges.

source.place: Proposition 3.7, total inversion special case; Section 3.2 signed-word presentation; agent-supplied comma-tree calculation

proof.text: For every nonempty finite connected subtree $H\subseteq T_b$ containing the root, prove that $N(P(H))\to *$ is a weak homotopy equivalence by induction on its number of vertices. A one-vertex tree has only its identity arrow, and its nerve is a point. Otherwise a longest simple path supplies a leaf $v$ different from the root; let $w$ be its unique neighbor and $H'=H\setminus\{v\}$. The inclusion $J:P(H')\to P(H)$ has a retraction $R$ sending $v$ to $w$, its incident edge to $1_w$, and fixing all other vertices and edges. This extends uniquely to words, so is a functor and $RJ=1$. If the edge points $v\to w$, there is a natural transformation $1\Rightarrow JR$ with this edge at $v$ and identities elsewhere. If it points $w\to v$, there is instead $JR\Rightarrow1$. For naturality, a directed path meeting a leaf can only start or finish there, and erasing the incident edge is exactly $R$; paths avoiding the leaf are fixed. The two functors therefore meet the hypotheses of [lem-coef-nerve-natural-homotopy-equivalence], which makes $NR$ a weak homotopy equivalence. The induction hypothesis and composition of weak equivalences from [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper] give the assertion for $H$. This includes either edge orientation.

source.place: Proposition 3.7; agent-supplied finite-tree contraction of the comma categories

proof.text: Let $\mathcal H_b$ be the poset of finite connected subtrees of $T_b$ containing its root. It is a small nonempty directed poset: it contains the root alone, and the union of two such subtrees is again finite, connected, and a subtree. A simplex of $N(P(T_b))$ is a finite string of finite directed edge paths, hence lies in the finite subtree obtained by adjoining to its finitely many vertices their unique finite paths to the root. Path-word equality is literal equality, so no two distinct simplices at a finite stage are identified at a larger stage. This proves $\operatorname{colim}_{H\in\mathcal H_b}N(P(H))=NE_b$, compatibly with deletion, composition, and identity insertion. The maps to the constant point diagram form a natural transformation of weak equivalences by Step 5. The filtered-colimit clause of [lem-coef-sset-gluing-filtered-equivalences] now gives $NE_b\to *$ a weak homotopy equivalence. The constant point diagram has colimit a point since the index poset is nonempty and directed.

source.place: Proposition 3.7; agent-supplied finite-subtree exhaustion, avoiding any local finiteness assumption

proof.text: For each $b$ of the small groupoid $G(P)$, Step 6 proves precisely the weak contractibility of the nerve of $(b\downarrow u)$. The left-aspherical nerve implication in [lem-coef-grothendieck-aspherical-base-change] therefore proves that the actual map $Nu:NP(Q)\to NG(P(Q))$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. This reasoning chooses $b$ only after fixing a target object, so imposes no connectedness condition on $Q$. If $O$ is empty, both nerves are empty and the canonical map is the identity. Apply this result to $Q_q$ from Step 1 for every $q$: the ordinary nerve maps $B(F)_{\bullet,q}\to B(G(F))_{\bullet,q}$ are weak homotopy equivalences. These maps form a morphism of bisimplicial sets because every simplicial operator of $F$ is a functor and the groupoid completion is functorial. The chosen generators need not be preserved by these operators.

source.place: Proposition 3.7, total inversion, and Proposition 9.2; agent-supplied Quillen-Theorem-A proof of the ordinary input

proof.text: Apply the exchanged-direction clause of [lem-coef-bisimplicial-diagonal-equivalence] to the weak equivalences $B(F)_{\bullet,q}\to B(G(F))_{\bullet,q}$ of Step 7. Its diagonal is precisely the canonical map $NF\to NG(F)$, so that map is a weak homotopy equivalence. By the universal property of groupoid completion, $i:C\to F$ and $p:F\to C$ extend functorially to $G(i)$ and $G(p)$, with $G(p)G(i)=1_{G(C)}$. Naturality of the completion maps gives commuting squares with $N(i),N(p),NG(i),NG(p)$. Thus $NC\to NG(C)$ is an arrow-category retract of $NF\to NG(F)$.

source.place: Proposition 9.2 and Section 1.4(vii): diagonal and retract argument

proof.text: To finish, the retract of a weak homotopy equivalence is one, directly from the definition in [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper]. Indeed, let $f:A\to B$ be a retract of $g:X\to Y$ with inclusions $i_A,i_B$ and retractions $r_A,r_B$. On path components, and on each based homotopy group at a basepoint $a\in|A|$ and its image in $|X|$, the inverse to the induced map of $f$ is $r_{A*}g_*^{-1}i_{B*}$. The two commuting retract squares and $r_*i_*=1$ make both its composites identities. Realization preserves these retract equations by functoriality. Applying this to Step 8 proves the required canonical map $NC\to NG(C)$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. If $O$ is empty the map is already the identity of the empty simplicial set. Isolated objects give singleton comma trees, and empty mapping sets and disconnected graphs are admitted throughout.
